title: kind vs minikube
description: A practical comparison of kind and minikube for running Kubernetes locally and in CI. Covers how each runs clusters, startup time, multi-node setups, add-ons, loading local images, LoadBalancer and ingress access, and which one to pick for development or pipelines.
introduction:
Sooner or later you need a Kubernetes cluster that is not production: to try a Helm chart, to debug a manifest, or to run integration tests on every pull request. kind and minikube are the two most common answers, and both come from Kubernetes SIGs, so neither is a toy.

They start from different goals. kind (Kubernetes IN Docker) was built to test Kubernetes itself. Every node is a container, clusters come up fast, and the whole thing is driven by a small config file, which is why it shows up in so many CI pipelines. minikube was built for developers learning and working with Kubernetes on a laptop. It can run the cluster in a VM or a container, and it ships add-ons like ingress, metrics-server and the dashboard that you turn on with one command.

In practice the gap has narrowed. minikube's docker driver runs the node as a container just like kind, and kind clusters can get ingress and LoadBalancer support with a bit of extra setup. The differences that still matter are around add-ons, networking to your host, multi-node configs and how well each fits a CI job.

This comparison walks through those differences, a set of common scenarios, and a quick decision matrix. If you mostly run tests in pipelines, you will probably end up on kind. If you want a local cluster that feels complete out of the box, minikube is the easier start.

toolA.name: kind
toolA.description: Kubernetes IN Docker. Runs each Kubernetes node as a container on Docker or Podman. Maintained by Kubernetes SIG Testing and used to test Kubernetes itself.
pros: Fast to create and delete clusters, which suits CI jobs
Multi-node and multi-control-plane clusters from a short YAML config
Light on resources since nodes are plain containers
First-class GitHub Actions support through helm/kind-action
Pick any Kubernetes version with a kindest/node image
cons: No built-in add-ons, so ingress, metrics-server and dashboards are manual installs
Reaching services from the host needs extraPortMappings or port-forward
LoadBalancer services need cloud-provider-kind or MetalLB
Requires Docker, Podman or nerdctl on the machine

toolB.name: minikube
toolB.description: A local Kubernetes tool from Kubernetes SIG Cluster Lifecycle. Runs a cluster in a VM or a container through drivers like docker, podman, kvm2, qemu, hyperv and virtualbox, with a catalogue of one-command add-ons.
pros: Add-ons for ingress, metrics-server, dashboard, registry and more with minikube addons enable
minikube tunnel gives LoadBalancer services a reachable IP
Choice of VM or container drivers, including setups without Docker
minikube docker-env lets you build images straight into the cluster
Choice of container runtime: docker, containerd or cri-o
cons: VM drivers are slower to start and reserve a fixed slice of CPU and memory
More moving parts to debug when a driver misbehaves
Heavier than kind for short-lived CI clusters
Multi-node clusters work but are less common in practice

toolB.value: Light with the docker driver, VM drivers reserve fixed CPU and memory

useCases.scenario: Running integration tests against a real cluster on every pull request in GitHub Actions
useCases.explanation: kind creates and deletes clusters quickly, needs nothing but Docker on the runner, and helm/kind-action sets it up in a couple of lines. Short-lived clusters per job are exactly what it was built for.

useCases.scenario: Learning Kubernetes and wanting ingress, metrics and a dashboard working on day one
useCases.explanation: minikube addons enable ingress and minikube dashboard get you a complete-feeling cluster without reading install docs for each component. With kind you would install and wire up each of those yourself.

useCases.scenario: Testing node drains, pod anti-affinity or a multi-control-plane setup
useCases.explanation: A kind config with three workers or three control-plane nodes is a few lines of YAML and comes up fast. You can tear it down and recreate it between experiments without much waiting.

useCases.scenario: A machine without Docker, or a need for a VM boundary around the cluster
useCases.explanation: minikube's kvm2, qemu, hyperv and virtualbox drivers run the cluster in a VM. kind always needs a container engine on the host.

useCases.scenario: Testing a Service of type LoadBalancer locally
useCases.explanation: minikube tunnel gives the service a reachable external IP with one command. On kind you need to run cloud-provider-kind or install MetalLB first.

useCases.scenario: Building an app image and iterating on it in a local cluster
useCases.explanation: Both can load a locally built image into the cluster: kind load docker-image on kind, minikube image load or docker-env on minikube. Set imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent or Never so the node does not try to pull it from a registry.

faqs.question: Can kind run without Docker?
faqs.answer: Yes. kind supports Podman and nerdctl as well. Set KIND_EXPERIMENTAL_PROVIDER=podman (or nerdctl) before creating the cluster. It still needs some container engine, so if you have none, minikube with a VM driver is the option.

faqs.question: Is either one meant for production?
faqs.answer: No. Both are for local development, testing and CI. For a small real cluster look at k3s, kubeadm or a managed service like EKS, GKE or AKS.

faqs.question: Can I run several clusters at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes on both. kind uses kind create cluster --name <name> and switches kubectl contexts per cluster. minikube uses profiles with minikube start -p <profile>.

faqs.question: Why does my pod show ErrImagePull for an image I just built?
faqs.answer: The cluster nodes do not share your host's image store. Load the image with kind load docker-image or minikube image load, and either avoid the :latest tag (it defaults imagePullPolicy to Always) or set imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent.

faqs.question: Which one does the Kubernetes project use for its own tests?
faqs.answer: kind. It came out of SIG Testing to run Kubernetes end-to-end tests in CI, and many upstream jobs still use it. That history is why it is so well suited to throwaway clusters in pipelines.

decisionMatrix.criteria: You need short-lived clusters in CI
You want ingress, metrics-server and a dashboard with no extra setup
You need multi-node or multi-control-plane clusters
You need to run without Docker or inside a VM
You want the lowest resource usage on your laptop
You just need a local cluster to apply manifests to

verdict.summary: kind is the better fit for CI and for anyone who wants fast, disposable, scriptable clusters, including multi-node ones. minikube is the friendlier local cluster, with add-ons, tunnels and VM drivers that save setup time when you are developing or learning. Many teams use both: minikube on laptops and kind in pipelines.
verdict.recommendation: Choose kind for CI pipelines, multi-node testing and minimal resource use. Choose minikube for day-to-day local development and learning, especially if you want ingress, LoadBalancer support or a dashboard without extra installs.
